questions.enonce_markdown:
The concept of death was a bone of contention in the Corinthian church. How valid is this statement?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** In 1 Corinthians there are several disputes among the believers at Corinth. Chapter 15 deals with a question related to death: some members were saying, "There is no resurrection of the dead" (15:12). The statement that the concept of death was a bone of contention can be tested against this chapter and other passages.

**1. The dispute in 1 Corinthians 15.**
- *The problem.* Some Corinthians accepted that Christ had been raised, but denied the future resurrection of believers. This reflects Greek thinking, in which the soul is immortal and the body is a prison or of little value, so a bodily resurrection seemed absurd (as at Athens, Acts 17:32).
- *Paul's answer.*
 - The resurrection of Christ is the heart of the gospel received and handed on. He lists those to whom the risen Lord appeared: Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred, James, all the apostles and finally Paul himself (15:3-8).
 - If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ has not been raised, preaching and faith are in vain, the believers are still in their sins, and those who have died in Christ have perished (15:12-19).
 - Christ is "the first fruits of those who have died"; as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive (15:20-23).
 - Death is "the last enemy" to be destroyed (15:26).
 - He refers to the practice of baptism on behalf of the dead (15:29) and to his own daily risks (15:30-32) as pointless if there is no resurrection.
 - To the question "How are the dead raised? With what kind of body?" he gives the analogy of the seed, and contrasts the physical body with the spiritual body (15:35-49).
 - The mystery: "We will not all die, but we will all be changed", at the last trumpet, and "Death has been swallowed up in victory" (15:51-55).

**2. Other contexts of death in the letter.** In the discussion of the Lord's Supper, Paul says that abuses at the meal have led to illness and that "some have died" (11:30), connecting the community's behaviour with judgement. Paul also speaks of the death of Christ as the heart of his message, which for the world is folly (1:18, 2:2).

**3. How valid is the statement?**
- *Valid:* the chapter shows that a serious disagreement existed, that Paul spends a very long argument on it, and that the Corinthian doubts were rooted in their culture.
- *Qualified:* the dispute was more about resurrection and the nature of life after death than about "death" as such. We know the Corinthian position only through Paul's reply, so its exact form is uncertain: some may have thought the resurrection had already happened spiritually, as in 2 Timothy 2:18. Also, death was only one of the contentious matters, with factions, immorality, lawsuits, idol meat, worship and spiritual gifts.

**Conclusion.** The statement is largely valid, as long as it is taken to mean the question of the resurrection of the dead. Paul answers it by grounding hope in the resurrection of Christ, and presents death as an enemy that God will defeat.
